title: The Loop Variable Is a Copy: Range-for, and What the Declaration Decides

questions.question: for (double v : values) v *= 2; is run over five readings that sum to 15. What do they sum to afterwards?
options: 15, since v is a copy of each reading and the doubled copy is thrown away
30, since every v was doubled
It does not compile, since v is modified
0, since v is destroyed at the end of each pass
questions.explanation: Measured: 15. The loop variable is declared by value, so it is a copy. Writing double& makes it the reading itself, and the sum becomes 30.

questions.question: A thousand Readings are visited with each of for (Reading r : ...), for (const Reading& r : ...), for (auto r : ...) and for (const auto& r : ...). How many copies does each make?
options: 1000, 0, 0, 0, since auto avoids copies
1000, 0, 1000, 0, since auto does not add a reference
0 for all four, since the compiler removes unnecessary copies
1000 for all four, since a range for always copies
questions.explanation: auto asks the compiler to write the type, and the type it writes has no reference in it unless you add one. Only the declarations with an & copy nothing.

questions.question: A function must return a pointer to the first reading above a limit. Its loop is for (Reading r : readings) and it returns &r. What is wrong?
options: It does not compile, since r is not a pointer
The pointer is to r, a copy that stops existing when the function returns
Nothing, &r is the address of the reading
It returns nullptr, since r is const
questions.explanation: It must be for (const Reading& r : readings). Measured from inside the loop: the address of a by value loop variable is different from the element's. The suite checks the returned pointer equals the address of the right element in the vector.

questions.question: In for (int x : Holder().items()), Holder() is a temporary and items() returns a reference into it. What happens?
options: The Holder lives until the end of the loop, so it is safe
The loop runs zero times
The Holder is destroyed before the body runs
It does not compile, since a temporary cannot be iterated
questions.explanation: The loop reads something already gone, which summed to 2882482050 with no error in a normal build. Measured: the count of destroyed holders was 1 when the body first ran. The address sanitizer reports stack-use-after-scope. Returning a copy by value is safe, because the copy is kept alive for the loop. C++23 changed the rule; this curriculum is on C++17.

questions.question: for (auto& flag : flags) will not compile when flags is a std::vector<bool>. Why?
options: Because vector<bool> packs flags into bits
Because flags is const
Because auto cannot be deduced for bool
Because vector<bool> cannot be iterated
questions.explanation: There is no bool to refer to and indexing hands back a temporary stand-in that a plain reference cannot bind to. The stand-in is 16 bytes on gcc 11, a pointer and a mask. for (auto flag : flags) works because it copies the stand-in, and writing to the flags is an index loop. Both compilers refuse the reference, which checks/ proves.

questions.question: Which loop variable is the right default when the loop only reads each element of a container of large structs?
options: Declared by pointer
Declared by value, since it is the simplest
auto&&, since it is the most general
const auto&, which copies nothing and cannot change the element
questions.explanation: Read with const auto&, change with auto&, and copy only something as cheap as a number. A double is fine by value; a struct holding a string or a vector is not.
